questions.question: What is the definition of the open metric ball $\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)$?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}:d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)\leq r\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}:d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0) \lt r\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\boldsymbol{X}:d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0) \gt r\}$
$\{r\in\mathbb{R}:d(r,\boldsymbol{x}_0) \lt \boldsymbol{x}\}$
questions.explanation: An open metric ball is the set of points whose distance from the centre is strictly less than the radius. The strict inequality $<$ is what makes it 'open'.

A subset is open if and only if it contains no open balls.
A subset is open if and only if it is finite.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the metric $d_1$, what is the shape of $\boldsymbol{B}((0,0),1)$?
options: A diamond with vertices $(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)$.
A usual circular disc
A square with vertices at $(\pm1,\pm1)$.
The whole plane
questions.explanation: The $d_1$ (Manhattan) metric on $\mathbb{R}^2$ uses $|x_1-x_2|+|y_1-y_2|$ as distance. The open unit ball around the origin is the set of points with $|x|+|y|<1$, which is a diamond shape with vertices at $(\pm1,0)$ and $(0,\pm1)$.
questions.source_support: Example in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $d_1$.
option_explanations: A circular disc is the Euclidean ($d_2$) ball, not the $d_1$ ball.
A square with vertices at $(\pm1,\pm1)$ would be the $d_\infty$ (max) ball, not the $d_1$ ball.
The whole plane would require an infinite radius, not radius $1$.
